title: Small ones count (Avot 2:1)
hookLine: Rabbi Judah: be as careful with a light commandment as a weighty one
carry: it will be well with you
last: JUSTICE THAT MAKES PEACE IN THE GATES.

lines: THE SHOPPING CART IN THE RAIN.
THE MAN WHO GATHERED THE MISHNAH.
cards: You'd run into a burning building for your family. Obviously. But would you hold the door for the stranger with the stroller?
Text back your aunt? Put the shopping cart back in the corral when it's raining? Most of us are ready for the big moments.

It's the small ones we skip, because surely they don't count for much. Chapter two of Pirkei Avot opens with the man who put the whole Mishnah together, and one of the first things he teaches is about the small ones.

teach.h: RABBI JUDAH, WHO GATHERED THE MISHNAH.
teach.b: He's Rabbi Judah the Prince, so respected that the Mishnah often just calls him Rabbi, as if there were only one.
Around the year two hundred, he gathered generations of oral teaching into the Mishnah, the book Pirkei Avot is part of.
His words: be as careful with a light commandment as with a weighty one, because you don't know the reward that's given for each.
The Torah has hundreds of commandments, and it almost never tells you what each one is worth. The rabbis say that's on purpose.

teach.h: NO PRICE LIST FOR THE COMMANDMENTS.
teach.b: If you knew the price list, you'd only do the expensive ones. Their example is hard to forget.

teach.h: THE MOTHER BIRD AND THE PARENTS.
teach.b: In Deuteronomy, if you find a bird's nest with the mother sitting on the eggs, you send the mother away before you take the eggs. It's one of the easiest commands in the Torah. It costs you nothing.

And the Torah attaches to it the promise that it will be well with you, and you'll have long days. That's the same promise given for honoring your father and mother, one of the hardest commandments there is.
The easiest and one of the hardest, the same reward. So don't sort your good deeds into ones that matter and ones that don't.

teach.h: WEIGH THE COST AND THE GAIN.
teach.b: Rabbi adds a kind of scale: weigh what a good deed costs you against what it brings, and what a wrong gains you against what it costs.
Small things are on that scale too. And you never know which small one is the heavy one.

how: Jewish practice gives attention to small commandments as well as great ones, and the command to send away the mother bird (shiluach haken) is often taught as the classic example of a 'light' mitzvah.

games.q: you have time for one more good deed today: a big one people will notice, or a small one nobody will. which counts more?
o: you can't know, so be careful with both.
games.why: Rabbi says be as careful with a light commandment as a weighty one, because you don't know the reward of each.

practice: Let your day come to mind, and look for the tiniest good thing in it you usually skip: refilling the water jug, saying thank you to the driver, answering a message from someone lonely.
Picture doing it with full attention, as if it were the most important thing you'll do today. Maybe it is; you don't know.
